items.stem: Name the two systems that control and coordinate activities in animals.
items.answer: The nervous system, which works by electrical impulses and acts quickly, and the endocrine system, which works by hormones carried in the blood and acts more slowly but for longer.

items.stem: What are receptors? Name two kinds.
items.answer: Receptors are specialised cells or organs that detect a change in the surroundings and start a nerve impulse. Photoreceptors in the eye detect light and phonoreceptors in the ear detect sound; gustatory and olfactory receptors detect taste and smell.

items.stem: What makes up the central nervous system?
items.answer: The brain and the spinal cord. They receive information, process it and send out instructions, while the peripheral nerves carry messages to and from them.

items.stem: Define tropism and name two kinds.
items.answer: Tropism is a directional growth movement of a plant part in response to an external stimulus. Phototropism is growth towards or away from light, and geotropism is growth in response to gravity; hydrotropism and chemotropism are further examples.

items.stem: Why is iodine essential in our diet?
items.answer: The thyroid gland needs iodine to make thyroxine, which controls the rate of metabolism. A shortage of iodine prevents enough thyroxine being made and causes the swelling of the neck known as goitre.

items.stem: What does the peripheral nervous system consist of, and what does it do?
items.answer: It consists of the cranial nerves arising from the brain and the spinal nerves arising from the spinal cord. It carries information from the receptors to the central nervous system and carries instructions from the central nervous system out to the muscles and glands.

items.stem: Why are reflex actions more useful than thinking in an emergency?
items.answer: Thinking involves the cerebrum and takes measurably longer, whereas a reflex arc routes the impulse through the spinal cord directly from the sensory to the motor neuron. In a situation such as touching something hot, that fraction of a second decides whether the tissue is damaged, so speed matters more than deliberation.

items.stem: How does the folding of a touch-me-not leaf differ from a shoot bending towards light?
items.answer: The folding is a nastic movement: it is rapid, caused by a sudden change of water content in the cells, independent of growth, and reversible, and its direction is unrelated to where the touch came from. The bending towards light is a tropic movement: it is slow, caused by unequal growth, permanent, and directed by the position of the stimulus.

items.stem: Describe the structure of a neuron and explain how an impulse travels along and between neurons.
items.answer: A neuron has three main parts. The cell body contains the nucleus and from it radiate short branched fibres called dendrites. A single long fibre called the axon leads away from the cell body and ends in fine branches called nerve endings. Information is picked up by the dendrites as a chemical change, which sets off an electrical impulse. The impulse travels along the dendrite to the cell body and then down the axon to its end. At the end of the axon the electrical impulse causes the release of a chemical, which crosses the tiny gap called the synapse and starts a fresh electrical impulse in the dendrite of the next neuron. The same kind of gap exists between a neuron and a muscle cell, which is how the instruction to contract is delivered. So transmission is electrical within a neuron and chemical between neurons, and because the chemical is released on one side only, the impulse can travel in one direction only.

items.stem: Name the three main parts of the human brain and state the function of each.
items.answer: The fore-brain, whose main part is the cerebrum, is the thinking part. It receives information from all the receptors, interprets it against what is already stored, and decides on a response; it also contains separate regions for hearing, smell, sight and for voluntary muscle action, and centres controlling hunger and thirst. The mid-brain, together with the hind-brain, deals with involuntary actions such as changes in pupil size and reflexes of the head and eyes. The hind-brain has three parts: the cerebellum, which coordinates precise voluntary movement and maintains posture and balance, so that we can walk in a straight line or ride a bicycle; the medulla, which controls involuntary actions including blood pressure, salivation and vomiting; and the pons, which regulates respiration. The brain is protected by the skull and by a fluid-filled cushion between the two.

items.stem: Trace the path of a reflex arc when a person steps on a sharp object.
items.answer: The pain receptors in the skin of the foot detect the stimulus and generate an impulse. The impulse travels along a sensory neuron to the spinal cord. Inside the spinal cord a relay neuron passes it directly to a motor neuron, without waiting for the brain. The motor neuron carries the impulse to the leg muscles, which contract and lift the foot away. Only after this has happened does a separate impulse travelling up the spinal cord reach the brain, which is why the person becomes conscious of the pain slightly after having already moved. The arrangement exists because the shortest path gives the fastest response, and in such a situation speed prevents injury. The spinal cord thus acts both as the site of the reflex and as the cable connecting the body to the brain.

items.stem: Name four endocrine glands, the hormone each secretes and one function of that hormone.
items.answer: The thyroid gland secretes thyroxine, which regulates the rate of carbohydrate, protein and fat metabolism and so the general rate of growth. The pancreas secretes insulin, which lowers blood sugar by helping cells take up glucose; too little insulin causes diabetes. The adrenal glands secrete adrenaline, which prepares the body for emergency by raising the heart rate and breathing rate and diverting blood to the muscles. The pituitary gland secretes growth hormone, which controls the growth and development of the body; too little in childhood causes dwarfism and too much causes gigantism. The testes secrete testosterone and the ovaries secrete oestrogen, which bring about the changes of puberty in males and females respectively.

items.stem: Name four plant hormones and state what each does.
items.answer: Auxin promotes the elongation of cells and is responsible for phototropism, since it accumulates on the shaded side of a shoot and makes those cells grow longer so the shoot bends towards the light. Gibberellin promotes stem elongation and helps seeds germinate. Cytokinin promotes cell division and is found in greatest concentration in regions of rapid division such as fruits and seeds. Abscisic acid inhibits growth, causes the wilting of leaves and helps close the stomata when water is short, so it acts in opposition to the other three. Unlike animal hormones, plant hormones are not made in special glands but are produced in the growing regions and move by diffusion from cell to cell.

items.stem: Explain why a nerve impulse travels in only one direction across a synapse.
items.answer: Within a neuron the impulse is electrical and could in principle travel either way along the fibre, but at the junction between two neurons the mechanism changes. The end of the axon of the first neuron contains vesicles of a chemical transmitter, and the arrival of the electrical impulse releases that chemical into the gap. The dendrite of the second neuron carries receptors that respond to the chemical and start a new electrical impulse. The asymmetry is structural: only the axon terminal can release the transmitter, and only the receiving membrane has the receptors. So a chemical released on one side finds receptors on the other but not the reverse, and an impulse arriving at the second neuron's axon terminal has no way to send a signal backwards across the same gap. This one-way arrangement is essential, since a nervous system in which impulses could travel in both directions at every junction would produce contradictory instructions and could not coordinate anything.

items.stem: Explain how the secretion of thyroxine is regulated, and why such regulation is necessary.
items.answer: Thyroxine controls the rate of metabolism, so its level must be held within narrow limits. The regulation works by negative feedback. When the level of thyroxine in the blood falls, the pituitary gland detects this and secretes more thyroid-stimulating hormone, which travels in the blood to the thyroid and makes it produce more thyroxine. As the thyroxine level rises, it acts back on the pituitary and suppresses the release of the stimulating hormone, so production falls again. The output is therefore continually corrected towards a set level, in the way a thermostat controls a heater. Such regulation is necessary because both excess and deficiency are harmful: too much thyroxine speeds metabolism, causing weight loss and a racing heart, while too little slows it, causing sluggishness and weight gain. It is also why the timing of secretion cannot be fixed in advance; the body's need varies with activity, diet and growth, so the gland must respond to the state of the blood rather than to a schedule. The same feedback principle controls insulin, where the stimulus is the blood glucose level itself.

items.stem: Compare nervous and hormonal control, and explain why an animal needs both.
items.answer: Nervous control uses electrical impulses carried along neurons. It is extremely fast, acting in milliseconds, it is precisely targeted at a particular muscle or gland through a definite physical connection, and its effect stops as soon as the impulse stops. Hormonal control uses chemicals released into the blood. It is slower, taking seconds to hours, it reaches every tissue the blood reaches so its targets are defined by which cells have receptors rather than by wiring, and its effects persist long after secretion. Neither alone would be sufficient. Nerves are needed for anything requiring speed and precision: withdrawing a hand, focusing an eye, coordinating the muscles of walking. But nerves cannot maintain a long-term state, because holding a signal for months would require continuous impulses to every affected cell. Hormones are needed for exactly those long-term, widespread processes: growth over years, the changes of puberty, the daily regulation of blood sugar and metabolism. The two also cooperate, as when a frightening sight is detected by the nervous system, which triggers the adrenal glands to release adrenaline, and the hormone then sustains the state of readiness long after the initial impulse has passed. So the division of labour is between speed and precision on one side and duration and breadth on the other.

items.answer: axon

items.answer: cerebrum

items.answer: goitre

items.stem: The growth of a root downwards in response to gravity is called ___________.
items.answer: geotropism

items.stem: Explain how the nervous system detects and responds to a stimulus, naming each stage.
items.answer: The process has five stages. First, detection: specialised receptor cells sense the change. Photoreceptors in the eye detect light, phonoreceptors in the ear detect sound, and receptors in the skin detect touch, pressure, heat and pain. Second, transmission to the centre: the receptor generates an electrical impulse which travels along a sensory neuron. Within the neuron the impulse passes from the dendrite through the cell body and down the axon; between neurons it crosses a gap called the synapse by means of a chemical. Third, processing: the impulse reaches the spinal cord or the brain. If the response must be immediate, a relay neuron in the spinal cord passes it straight to a motor neuron, and this short circuit is called a reflex arc. If the response requires thought, the impulse travels to the cerebrum, which interprets it against stored information and decides what to do. Fourth, transmission to the effector: a motor neuron carries the instruction out to a muscle or a gland. Fifth, response: the effector acts, the muscle contracting or the gland secreting. The whole sequence can be completed in a fraction of a second, which is what allows an animal to react to a changing world.

items.stem: Describe the endocrine system of the human body, naming the main glands and their hormones and effects.
items.answer: The endocrine system consists of ductless glands that release hormones directly into the blood, which carries them to their target organs. The pituitary gland, beneath the brain, secretes growth hormone, which controls the growth of bones and tissues; too little in childhood causes dwarfism and too much causes gigantism. It also controls several other glands. The thyroid gland, in the neck, secretes thyroxine, which regulates the rate at which carbohydrates, proteins and fats are used; it requires iodine, and a dietary shortage causes goitre. The adrenal glands, above the kidneys, secrete adrenaline in an emergency, which raises the heart rate and breathing rate, diverts blood from the digestive system to the muscles and raises blood glucose, preparing the body for action. The pancreas secretes insulin, which lowers blood sugar by helping cells take up glucose; a failure to produce enough causes diabetes, treated by insulin injection. The testes secrete testosterone, which brings about the deepening of the voice and growth of facial hair at puberty, and the ovaries secrete oestrogen, which brings about breast development and regulates the menstrual cycle. Secretion of each hormone is controlled by feedback, so that its level in the blood is held within narrow limits rather than being fixed in advance.

items.stem: Explain what a reflex arc is, why it evolved, and how it differs from a voluntary action.
items.answer: A reflex arc is the pathway followed by an impulse in a reflex action. The receptor detects the stimulus and sends an impulse along a sensory neuron to the spinal cord. There a relay neuron passes it directly to a motor neuron, which carries it to the effector muscle, and the muscle contracts. The brain is informed afterwards but is not part of the arc. As to why it evolved, the reason is speed. Thinking involves the cerebrum, which must receive the information, interpret it and decide, and that takes measurably longer. In the situations reflexes handle, such as touching a hot object, a dust particle entering the eye or something flying at the face, a fraction of a second decides whether damage is done, so a shortcut that bypasses deliberation is worth having. It is also likely that reflexes came first in evolutionary terms and that the thinking process was added later, which is why the spinal cord retains this capability rather than everything being routed through the brain. A reflex differs from a voluntary action in several ways. It is involuntary and cannot easily be prevented, whereas a voluntary action is chosen. It is fast and stereotyped, giving the same response to the same stimulus every time, whereas a voluntary response can vary with circumstances. It is controlled by the spinal cord, whereas voluntary action is controlled by the cerebrum. And it requires no learning, whereas many voluntary actions must be learnt, though with practice some learnt actions such as cycling become almost automatic through the cerebellum.

items.stem: Compare control and coordination in plants and animals, and assess whether plants are at a disadvantage.
items.answer: Animals coordinate using two systems. The nervous system carries electrical impulses along neurons, giving responses in milliseconds that are precisely targeted through physical connections. The endocrine system carries hormones in the blood, giving slower but longer-lasting effects across the whole body. Animals also possess muscle tissue, so they can move rapidly and can move the whole organism. Plants have neither nerves nor muscles. They coordinate entirely by chemical messengers called phytohormones, which are not made in glands but in growing regions, and which travel by diffusion from cell to cell rather than in a circulatory system. Their responses are correspondingly slow, taking hours or days, and they take the form of growth rather than movement: a shoot bends towards light by growing unevenly, a root grows downwards, a tendril coils around a support. A few faster responses exist, such as the folding of a touch-me-not leaf, but these work by sudden changes in the water content of cells and are not typical. Whether this is a disadvantage depends on what is being compared. For escaping a predator or catching prey, plainly yes, and plants have instead evolved thorns, toxins and the ability to regrow from damage. But for a stationary organism the requirement is different. A plant must grow towards light and water over weeks, shed leaves before a dry season and open and close stomata as conditions change, and a slow, growth-based, chemically coordinated system does all of this economically, without the heavy cost of maintaining nerves and muscles. The fair conclusion is not that plants are worse coordinated but that the two solutions match two quite different ways of living.

items.stem: A nerve impulse travels at 100 metres per second. How long does it take to travel 1.5 metres from the foot to the spinal cord?
items.answer: Time equals distance divided by speed, that is 1.5 divided by 100, which is 0.015 seconds, or 15 milliseconds. This is why a reflex feels instantaneous.

items.stem: A reflex response takes 20 milliseconds while a voluntary response to the same stimulus takes 200 milliseconds. Express the difference as a factor and comment.
items.answer: The voluntary response takes 200 divided by 20, that is 10 times as long as the reflex. The difference of 180 milliseconds may sound small, but for a hand on a hot surface it is the difference between a reddened skin and a blister, since damage accumulates throughout the contact. This is precisely why the reflex arc bypasses the brain: the saving is not in energy but in time, and time is what prevents the injury.

items.stem: A person's fasting blood glucose is 180 mg per 100 mL against a normal upper limit of 110. Find the excess as a percentage and explain what it suggests.
items.answer: The excess is 180 minus 110, which is 70 mg per 100 mL. As a percentage of the normal upper limit this is 70 divided by 110, times 100, which is about 64 per cent above the limit. A fasting level this far above normal suggests that glucose is not being taken up by the cells, which points to insufficient insulin being produced by the pancreas or to the cells responding poorly to it, the condition called diabetes mellitus. The reasoning depends on the measurement being a fasting one, since a level taken shortly after a meal would be high in a healthy person too, and a single reading would need confirming before any conclusion is drawn.

items.stem: Match each brain part in Column I with its function in Column II. Column I: (a) cerebrum, (b) cerebellum, (c) medulla, (d) hypothalamus. Column II: (i) hunger and thirst, (ii) thinking and memory, (iii) heartbeat and blood pressure, (iv) balance and posture.
items.answer: (a) cerebrum - (ii) thinking and memory. (b) cerebellum - (iv) balance and posture. (c) medulla - (iii) heartbeat and blood pressure. (d) hypothalamus - (i) hunger and thirst.

items.stem: Match each gland in Column I with its hormone in Column II. Column I: (a) thyroid, (b) pancreas, (c) adrenal, (d) pituitary. Column II: (i) insulin, (ii) growth hormone, (iii) thyroxine, (iv) adrenaline.
items.answer: (a) thyroid - (iii) thyroxine, controlling metabolic rate. (b) pancreas - (i) insulin, lowering blood sugar. (c) adrenal - (iv) adrenaline, preparing the body for action. (d) pituitary - (ii) growth hormone, controlling growth.

items.stem: Draw a labelled diagram of a reflex arc and mark the direction of the impulse.
items.answer: Draw a cross-section of the spinal cord as an oval with a butterfly-shaped grey region inside it. On the left, draw the skin of a hand with a receptor and label it receptor in the skin. Draw a sensory neuron running from the receptor into the back of the spinal cord and label it sensory neuron, with its cell body shown in a swelling just outside the cord, the dorsal root ganglion. Inside the grey matter, draw a short relay neuron and label it relay neuron. From it draw a motor neuron leaving the front of the cord and running to a muscle in the arm, labelling both motor neuron and effector muscle. Mark arrowheads along the whole pathway showing the direction: receptor, sensory neuron, spinal cord, relay neuron, motor neuron, muscle. Label each junction between two neurons as a synapse. Add a separate arrow running upwards inside the spinal cord towards the brain, labelled impulse to the brain, and annotate it to say that the brain is informed only after the muscle has already acted. Add a final note that the brain is not part of the arc, which is what makes the response fast.

items.stem: Draw a labelled diagram of a neuron and annotate it to show how an impulse is received, carried and passed on.
items.answer: Draw a cell body as a rounded shape containing a nucleus, with several short branched fibres radiating from it. Label the cell body and label the branched fibres dendrites. From one side of the cell body draw a single long fibre and label it axon, showing a segmented covering along its length labelled myelin sheath. At the far end, draw the axon splitting into several fine branches with small swellings at their tips, and label these nerve endings or axon terminals. Beside them draw the dendrite of a second neuron with a narrow gap between, and label the gap synapse. Now annotate the sequence with numbered arrows. At the dendrites, note that information is acquired as a chemical change which sets off an electrical impulse. Along the dendrite and cell body, note that the impulse travels towards the axon. Along the axon, note that the impulse travels electrically, and against the myelin sheath note that it insulates the fibre and speeds conduction. At the axon terminal, note that the electrical impulse releases a chemical into the synapse. Across the gap, note that the chemical diffuses and starts a fresh electrical impulse in the next neuron. Add a final annotation that because only the axon terminal releases the chemical and only the receiving dendrite has receptors, the impulse can cross in one direction only.

items.stem: Describe an experiment to prove that a shoot grows towards light, and that the response is caused by light rather than by gravity or air movement.
items.answer: Take two identical potted seedlings grown in the dark so that neither has yet been exposed to directional light. Place the first in a cardboard box with a single small window cut in one side, so that light can enter from one direction only. Place the second in an identical box with the window covered but with holes for ventilation at the top and bottom, so that air can circulate but no light enters. Keep both boxes upright, side by side, at the same temperature, and water both equally. Leave them for two to three days. The seedling in the box with the open window bends distinctly towards the window. The seedling in the dark box grows straight upwards without bending in any direction. Now test the two alternative explanations. Gravity cannot account for the bending, because both boxes were upright, so gravity acted identically on both, and only one bent; furthermore the bend was sideways, towards the window, not along the direction of gravity. Air movement cannot account for it either, because the second box was ventilated and its seedling did not bend, and as a further check the first experiment can be repeated with the box turned so that the window faces the opposite way, when the seedling bends the other way, following the light rather than any fixed feature of the room. Since the only variable that differed between the two boxes was the presence of directional light, and reversing the light reverses the bend, the response is caused by light. The response is a tropism rather than a mere movement because the bending results from unequal growth: auxin accumulates on the shaded side and makes those cells elongate more, so the stem curves towards the lit side, and the change is permanent rather than reversible.
